title: Provably efficient experimental classification of quantum data with quantum kernels
authors: Keitaro Anai, Akimoto Nakayama, Shintaro Ooka, Hiroko Tomoda, Yuto Morohoshi, Yohji Chin, Shigehito Miki, Masahiro Yabuno, Hirotaka Terai, Peter van Loock, Kosuke Mitarai, Shuntaro Takeda
abstract: Analyzing quantum systems is essential for quantum information processing, but can require exponentially many measurements without exploiting the structure of the system or task. Quantum machine learning offers a promising way to reduce this cost by learning from quantum data. Here, we theoretically establish a framework for efficient quantum-state classification and experimentally demonstrate the resulting scheme on a programmable photonic processor. Our analysis links learning efficiency to the structure of quantum data, without relying on a physical description tailored to each task. We derive sufficient conditions for accurate classification with a number of measurements polynomial in system size. We apply this guarantee to a resource problem in continuous-variable (CV) quantum computing: classifying stellar rank, a measure of non-Gaussianity. Experimentally, we implement the classification of single-mode CV quantum states with stellar rank zero and one. This is enabled by developing a programmable CV photonic processor capable of preparing and processing diverse Gaussian and non-Gaussian states and performing virtual projection onto such states, going beyond the Gaussian-only capabilities of most existing photonic platforms. The experiment demonstrates accurate classification despite experimental imperfections. Our results establish a theory-guided and experimentally validated framework for quantum-state classification that can be implemented on quantum devices available today.
summary: This paper presents a theory-guided framework for efficiently classifying quantum states using quantum kernel methods, bypassing the need for exponentially complex measurements. The authors theoretically prove polynomial resource scaling and experimentally demonstrate this scheme by classifying the stellar rank of continuous-variable quantum states using a programmable photonic processor.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of efficiently classifying quantum states without requiring an exponentially large number of measurements, a necessity for practical quantum machine learning.
main_result: They establish a theory-guided framework guaranteeing classification accuracy with a number of measurements polynomial in system size, which was experimentally validated on a photonic processor.
method: The core method uses quantum kernel methods, specifically the quantum Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel derived from quantum fidelities, framed as a Support-Vector-Machine classifier.
model_or_system: The experiments are performed on a programmable photonic processor capable of generating and processing continuous-variable (CV) quantum states, specifically classifying single-mode states based on their stellar rank (a measure of non-Gaussianity).
key_observables: Classification accuracy, quantum fidelity ($|\langle\psi_j|\psi_iangle|^2$), and the stellar rank of the quantum states.
important_parameters: The theoretical guarantee relies on the margin $\eta$ being bounded below by an inverse polynomial in system size $m$. Experimentally, the setup uses specific squeezing levels and measurement parameters ($\alpha,  eta$).
main_assumptions: The theoretical guarantee assumes the class does not collapse onto its representatives. Experimentally, the method is shown to be robust despite experimental imperfections.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the conceptual framework (Fig 1), the mode-number dependence of classification accuracy comparing different kernels (Fig 2), measured fidelities (Fig 3), and the comparison of classification accuracy vs. training set size (Fig 4).
paper_structure: The paper first theoretically establishes the framework linking learning efficiency to data structure, deriving polynomial resource bounds. It then applies this to the resource problem of stellar rank classification in CV states. The latter part details the experimental implementation, including the measurement procedures for estimating quantum fidelities using homodyne detection on a photonic platform.
why_interesting: The work provides a concrete, experimentally validated blueprint for implementing quantum machine learning tasks on current photonic hardware, moving beyond purely theoretical bounds by addressing resource scaling.
